title: Plumbline: is it still what it claims to be?

fonts.display: Iowan Old Style, Palatino Linotype, Georgia, serif
fonts.body: Segoe UI, system-ui, Helvetica Neue, Arial, sans-serif

beats.line: An agentic website ships an agent that runs in every visitor's browser. Once it's live, nobody checks it again. Plumbline does.
It checks any site, live, with three independent checkers. Here, one of them has no answer, so the verdict is unavailable. Never a quiet pass.
Here are three examples: a guesthouse, a clinic, and the agent that writes your code.
Larch House is a small guesthouse. Its website's agent tells guests a double room costs eighty-nine euros.
The owner raises the price to ninety-five on the page, and nobody tells the agent.
Plumbline's daily watch reads the page against what was locked, and says it plainly: the assistant may still be quoting eighty-nine euros, where the page now says ninety-five.
The Desk is an agentic website itself. Its assistant runs the same reading, and answers the owner in plain words.
All it took was one command. No key, and no account.
Now, Northgate Clinic. It signs its agent files with a key only the clinic holds, and before anything is signed, the page lists every file and its fingerprint.
A pharmacy that works with the clinic checks those files. At first the answer is unverifiable: it has never met this key.
It compares the key with the clinic by phone, trusts it once, and the clinic's files verify.
Then a copycat site serves the clinic's agent, signed with the clinic's stolen key. It's still refused: the signature names the clinic's address, not this one.
And Plumbline shows what the copy changed: repeat prescriptions now go to the copycat, with the patient's date of birth and NHS number.
Edit one file on the clinic's own site and the verdict is invalid: tampered. Verified says who published the files, never that a site is safe.
Last, the agent that writes your code. Plumbline pins its instructions, its settings, and every tool its servers offer, and a named person approves them.
One morning a tool server ships an update. Its search tool now tells the agent to read a private key and send it along.
The guard hides the changed tool and refuses the call, so the agent never reads those words.
In the pull request the check fails, and the new sentence sits in the diff until an approver reads it.
A guesthouse, a clinic, a coding agent. Plumbline keeps each one what its owner approved, and says plainly when it can't tell. Thanks for watching.
